Templates: knowledge-*

Node types: knowledge-goal, knowledge-decision, knowledge-option, knowledge-action, knowledge-outcome, knowledge-observation — six templates, one file, per the family-file convention
File naming: this file is knowledge.template.html, named after the knowledge-* family it defines, the same way spec.template.html names the spec-* family
Purpose: deciduous's node schema, reimplemented as templates instead of one flat SQL table — the proof case DESIGN.html proposed
Sibling of: spec.template.html, the spec-* family
Styling: ./knowledge.template.css, this family's own rendering rules, plus the shared ../theme.css every document links

Why six templates, not one flat schema

deciduous's git-native cousin hive discovered mid-build that status only makes sense for goal/decision/action, not for option/outcome/observation, and had to bolt on a nodeTypeSupportsStatus() helper to fake per-type shape onto one flat SQL table. Here that isn't a workaround: knowledge-goal declares a knowledge-status field, knowledge-observation simply doesn't. Six separate <template> entries in one knowledge-*-named file, exactly as DESIGN.html's own worked example already showed for this same schema.

Shared field vocabulary

Every type shares only the family prefix on its fields, not its own type name (knowledge-title, not knowledge-goal-title) — see the design spec's naming section. Two fields need more than "present and non-empty":

  • knowledge-confidence — an integer 0–100, matching deciduous's own -c/--confidence flag.
  • knowledge-status — one of pending, active, completed, rejected. This resolves the open question the design spec left: deciduous's own CLI (deciduous status --help) defines exactly these four, not the draft/approved/implemented enum spec-doc uses for an unrelated reason (that one tracks the brainstorming skill's lifecycle, not deciduous's).

knowledge-prompt is optional even on knowledge-goal: CLAUDE.md's own rule is that a verbatim prompt belongs on root goals and major direction changes, not on every downstream node, so a knowledge-goal without one is valid, not incomplete.

Both of these rules — and every other type's required/optional fields — are now expressed as required/pattern/enum attributes directly on each type's own <template> below, read generically by template.template.html's validator, rather than as hand-written per-type JS.

The six types

knowledge-goal

What the user asked for. Fields: title, confidence, status, optional prompt (the verbatim request, for root goals and major direction changes), optional detail.

<knowledge-goal data-conforms-to="./knowledge.template.html#knowledge-goal">
  <knowledge-title>Build v4: knowledge graph as hypermedia</knowledge-title>
  <knowledge-confidence>85</knowledge-confidence>
  <knowledge-status>active</knowledge-status>
  <knowledge-prompt>we are playing around with mycelium…</knowledge-prompt>
</knowledge-goal>

knowledge-decision

A choice made between approaches. Fields: title, confidence, status, optional detail.

<knowledge-decision data-conforms-to="./knowledge.template.html#knowledge-decision">
  <knowledge-title>HTML documents as canonical store, not DB + Markdown</knowledge-title>
  <knowledge-confidence>80</knowledge-confidence>
  <knowledge-status>active</knowledge-status>
</knowledge-decision>

knowledge-option

One alternative considered within a decision. No status — the option was or wasn't chosen, that's what an edge to its parent decision says, not a lifecycle of its own. Linked to its parent with <a data-rel="depends_on">, the closest of the six edge labels. Fields: title, confidence, optional detail.

<knowledge-option data-conforms-to="./knowledge.template.html#knowledge-option">
  <knowledge-title>Keep the six-file split (one template file per type)</knowledge-title>
  <knowledge-confidence>40</knowledge-confidence>
  <a data-rel="depends_on" href="./knowledge.template.html">considered for this file, rejected in favor of one bundled file</a>
</knowledge-option>

knowledge-action

About to write or edit code. Fields: title, confidence, status, optional detail, optional commit/files/branch once it's tied to real work.

<knowledge-action data-conforms-to="./knowledge.template.html#knowledge-action">
  <knowledge-title>Write DESIGN.html</knowledge-title>
  <knowledge-confidence>90</knowledge-confidence>
  <knowledge-status>completed</knowledge-status>
  <knowledge-commit>9794442</knowledge-commit>
  <knowledge-branch>main</knowledge-branch>
</knowledge-action>

knowledge-outcome

Something worked or failed. No status — an outcome is the record of what happened, not a thing that has a lifecycle itself. Fields: title, confidence, optional detail, optional commit/files/branch.

<knowledge-outcome data-conforms-to="./knowledge.template.html#knowledge-outcome">
  <knowledge-title>DESIGN.html written and committed</knowledge-title>
  <knowledge-confidence>92</knowledge-confidence>
  <knowledge-commit>9794442</knowledge-commit>
</knowledge-outcome>

knowledge-observation

Something noticed along the way, not yet a decision. Fields: title, confidence, optional detail.

<knowledge-observation data-conforms-to="./knowledge.template.html#knowledge-observation">
  <knowledge-title>Removing the <style> block made every document read like structured data</knowledge-title>
  <knowledge-confidence>70</knowledge-confidence>
</knowledge-observation>

Edges

The six data-rel labels deciduous already uses: depends_on, blocks, supports, contradicts, alternative_to, leads_to, written the same way DESIGN.html's own example shows: <a data-rel="leads_to" href="./outcome-x.html">…</a>. This project's own chain tonight used leads_to for its forward narrative (goal → decision → action → outcome → action) and depends_on for knowledge-option → parent knowledge-decision, the closest existing label for that relationship.

A worked example

One sample instance per type, checked by template.template.html's generic validator, per the attributes on each type's own <template> above. Wired together with real data-rel edges, not just sitting side by side — the graph-wide audits below read this exact markup, nothing hand-typed.

They are real instances, not illustrations. mycelium validate finds them by their data-conforms-to the same way it finds every instance in the corpus, so this file fails if one stops conforming.

Sample goal 85 active leads to the sample decision Sample decision 80 pending leads to the sample action Sample option 40 considered for the sample decision Sample action 90 completed abc1234 Sample action with no detail and no commit, written across several source lines so it also shows a title being measured as collapsed text 60 completed edged on purpose, so it stays out of the orphan audit Sample outcome 92 deliberately outgoing-only, see the audits below Sample observation 70

Graph-wide audits

DESIGN.html makes the case that a graph-wide audit isn't a separate constraint language, it's a script — the same kind of script that validates one instance against one template, just pointed at the whole node/edge set instead of one element. These four live here, next to the six types, rather than in a file of their own: each only ever concerns knowledge-* types, a family already bundled in this one file, so there's nothing to link across and nothing gained by separating them. A future audit that spans two families — say, checking a spec-doc's specifies edge actually resolves to a real knowledge-action — would earn its own file, since neither family's template file could host it without redeclaring the other's types. None of the audits below is that.

Two of them ask about edges (orphans-except-goal, dangling-outcome) and one asks about the shape of a single node's own fields (hollow-action). There used to be a second of that kind, title-length, and it is now a pattern on the field itself: a check belongs in the schema once the schema can say it. hollow-action stays because "at least one of these two fields" is not something the vocabulary can express, and the alternative was adding a word to the engine for one type's benefit.

The convention: data-validates="#id" marks a script checking one instance against one template, through check(root). data-audits="name" marks a script checking the whole graph, through check(fs), where fs is a read-only AuditFs that lists, reads and parses files on demand. The engine hands over the tree rather than a pre-built graph, so extraction stays the audit's own job, and its root sits one level above docs/ so a check can reach src/ as well.

data-touches lists which types an audit concerns, queryable the same way data-rel makes an edge queryable, instead of leaving it as prose only a person reading this paragraph would know.

orphans-except-goal

CLAUDE.md: "Root goal nodes are the ONLY valid orphans." Every node whose type isn't knowledge-goal must appear in at least one edge, incoming or outgoing.

dangling-outcome

CLAUDE.md: "Does every outcome link back to what caused it?" Deliberately stricter than orphan-checking: an outcome with only an outgoing edge (it leads somewhere, but nothing resolved into it) would already pass orphans-except-goal, yet still be exactly the dangling case CLAUDE.md's checklist means. So this checks specifically for an incoming edge, the way this project's own action →leads_to→ outcome links have worked all night.

Title length is declared, not audited

A knowledge-title past 140 characters is a paragraph filed in the wrong field: the finding is still legible, but it can't be scanned in a list, and whatever nuance it carries is invisible to anything that reads titles as labels. knowledge-detail is where that text belongs, and has been since the field existed.

This used to be an audit called title-length, walking the whole corpus. It is now pattern="^.{1,140}$" on each type's own knowledge-title above.

The rule did not change; where it lives did. A maximum length is a property of one field on one node, and the schema vocabulary could already say it, so saying it in code was writing by hand what the template could declare. See the decision, which also explains why hollow-action below did not move: it needs a word the vocabulary does not have, and adding one to serve a single type is growing the engine rather than using it.

140 is a judgment, not a boundary found in the data. Measured over the whole graph on 2026-07-30, the count fell smoothly — 61 nodes over 100 characters, 47 over 140, 17 over 300, median 84, p90 302. There is no knee to calibrate against, so no threshold here can be justified by the distribution; 140 is picked as "about two lines of a title" and should be argued with on those terms rather than defended as empirical. Those 47 have since been rewritten; the longest title in the corpus is now 135.

A regex can only express this because the generic validator collapses whitespace before testing. 14 of those 47 titles wrapped across source lines, and against raw text a length regex counts the indentation and the newlines as content. The longest title measured 139 that way against its real 135, four characters from a limit it was nowhere near. Collapsing is what makes a declared length mean the same thing as the audit's measured one.

Two costs, since neither is visible from the attribute. The limit is now written once per type rather than once in total, so changing it is six edits and nothing checks that the six agree. And audits skip templates/ while per-instance validation does not, so the sample instance below can no longer carry a deliberately over-long title to demonstrate the rule — it would fail its own template. It keeps the wrapping, which still shows collapsed measurement, and drops the length.

hollow-action

A knowledge-action with neither a non-empty knowledge-detail nor a knowledge-commit asserts that work happened without saying what it was or pointing at the diff — it is either redundant with git or empty. Either field alone clears it: CLAUDE.md's own rule says an action spanning several commits should omit the hash, so the detail carries it instead.

Deliberately not a required field on the knowledge-action template. Requiring both outright would reject the legitimate shapes (an action mid-flight has no commit yet); requiring either one is a property of the pair, which a per-field required attribute can't express and this audit can.

What the audits above are aimed at

The samples are wired so that extraction produces exactly one violation per audit: sample-observation has no edges at all, sample-outcome has only an outgoing edge (to sample-action) with nothing pointing into it, and sample-hollow-action carries neither a detail nor a commit. That last one also has an outgoing depends_on edge purely so it doesn't show up in orphans-except-goal as well and change what it asserts.

Each audit names its own violation in data-expects, and that is what makes these samples safe to leave in the corpus the real run sees. mycelium validate hands every audit every document, this file included, and compares what an audit finds against what it declares. A violation nobody declared fails the run. A declared one that stops appearing also fails it, which is the useful half: give sample-hollow-action a detail and the build tells you this demo has stopped demonstrating anything, rather than quietly passing.

The demo below reads data-expects off the audits rather than keeping its own list, so the browser and the build check the same declaration. Two copies could disagree, and the one that would go on saying PASS is this one.

Graph extraction, in a file

extractGraph(documents) lives in extract-graph.ts, beside this file, and all three of its callers import it: the two graph-consuming audits above (orphans-except-goal and dangling-outcome — hollow-action reads fields rather than edges, so it never needs a graph at all) and the generate command below.

It was embedded here until the in-page demos were removed, and each of those two audits carried its own copy rather than importing. That was not preference.

An audit also ran in a demo that loaded it from a data: URL, and a data: URL module has no base to resolve an import against, so an audit that imported anything would have broken the demo — the same reasoning duplicate-not-share-loadcheck gave for a smaller case. With the demo gone the constraint goes, and the copies with it. See the spec for why this became a file rather than a script carrying an id.

Authoring commands

add and link, declared once for the whole family — see the design spec for why this is one script per template file rather than one per command or per type, and why type="mycelium/command" instead of type="module". Never run in a browser: no live demo below, unlike every data-audits script above. Each command's own /** … */ comment is its only documentation — mycelium knowledge --help (or an unrecognized command) prints every exported command's name and doc comment straight from this file, so the usage shown here and the usage the CLI reports can never drift apart.
